title: He couldn't defeat addiction demons
article: There were actually two Grant Spielmachers, both struggling to survive on a nearly forgotten fringe of society.
One was a brash but kind Spielmacher, possessed of an impish sense of humour and enjoying above all else the profoundly simple pleasure of a friend's company.

The other Spielmacher was manifested by the hot taste of liquor or the numbing buzz of glue fumes. Angry, confused and tormented by violence and the darkness of addiction, he routinely found himself drying out as a guest of the Niagara Detention Centre.

It was that side of Spielmacher, the one that gnawed upon his weaknesses, that led to his arrest for public drunkenness in downtown St. Catharines Monday night. While in the custody of Niagara Regional Police, the 45-year-old died and a provincial investigation into his death has been launched.

To the 40 people gathered at Knox Presbyterian Church Friday night, Spielmacher was not remembered as a drunk who lived in a one- room apartment and died in a jail cell. Especially not to his foster mother, who above all else wants people to remember that he was a person and was loved. That he struggled with the same demons everyone else does. That he will not be forgotten.

"He was my first child," said Margaret Gruber, who took in a troubled 13-year-old Spielmacher while living in Kitchener. "We loved him and he loved us very much. And if you have someone who cares about you, then you have made a difference."

From the beginning, Spielmacher's life was a struggle. He was one of five children from a chaotic and violent home. At the age of 10, he entered the labyrinth of addiction by sniffing glue and never really found his way out.

"Living with him was sometimes very difficult," Gruber said before the funeral service at the church Friday night. "But when he wasn't ripped, he had this wonderful sense of humour. You just couldn't stop laughing, he was so funny."
Gruber and her husband Klaus both worked with troubled teens professionally and tried to help Spielmacher defeat his demons. They vowed never to send him away.
But three years after he moved in, they found living with him and his addictions impossible.
"I helped him move out properly. He found a place to live and work in factories and so on," she said.
That they had to ask him to leave has haunted Gruber for years, even after they moved from Ontario to Saskatoon where they now live.
"We were very, very depressed because we thought we didn't make a difference to his life at all."

On the surface, it certainly seemed that way. He left Kitchener in his 20s and moved to St. Catharines to escape the influence of a bad crowd. But some vices cannot be so easily escaped, even with the help of mental-health workers.

His addiction to glue-sniffing was exacerbated by alcohol and drugs. He had a girlfriend and fathered a daughter, but Spielmacher's problems were too much for them and they left. He knew first-hand the toll violence has on a soul, but could unleash a terrible rage when drunk.
He wrote letters to the Grubers regularly and they visited him at least once a year. Through the letters she learned he was arrested more than once.
But six weeks ago, after being released from the detention centre, Spielmacher placed a call to the Grubers at the suggestion of a mental-health worker.
"I know you already know it, but I wanted to tell you what you and Klaus mean to me, and how much I love you both," he told his former foster mother.
It was the last time she heard his voice.
But to Gruber, that call proved that the Spielmacher who made her laugh until her sides hurt hadn't been lost despite his troubles.
"It was very hard to watch him struggle so much," she said. "But he struggled with a smile on his face."
The cause of his death hasn't been released. An autopsy was performed Friday, but the results haven't been made available yet.
